videos.question: How do I help my parents plan a move when they don't know where to start?
videos.card: Parents thinking about moving? Where to start
videos.short: Start with a strategy session: no commitment to sell, just a conversation about what the home could sell for and what is worth doing before a move. Heading into winter there is time to make a plan, a few indoor repairs and some decluttering, one manageable job at a time, and just as important, what they don't need to spend time or money on. Instead of one overwhelming move, they get a clear checklist and decide on their own time.
videos.transcript:
Are your parents talking about moving, but one look around the home and you know they have no idea where to start? Now, you don't want to rush them, but you do want them to understand what comes next, and that's where a strategy session can help. No commitment to sell, just a conversation about what the home could sell for and what's worth doing before a move.

Now, heading into winter, there's more time to make a plan. A few indoor repairs, some decluttering, one manageable job at a time. And just as important, what they don't need to spend time or money on. So instead of one overwhelming move, they have a clear checklist and can decide on their own time. So if the house does become harder to manage this winter, they already have a head start.

Would your parents be relieved if they had a plan? If so, send me a DM and let's start there.

videos.question: Where are Ontario home prices headed, according to CREA's new forecast?
videos.card: Where are home prices headed next?
videos.short: CREA now expects Ontario home prices to finish the year down 3%, and that lines up with what Jonathan Wallace is seeing on the ground: it will probably get a little worse before it gets better. Fixed mortgage rates are rising and the big banks and investors expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates over the next year. Deals right now lean in the buyer's favour. CREA expects things to pick up in 2027, so if you're buying this could be your window, and if you're selling, price it right from day one.
videos.transcript:
CREA just updated its housing forecast, and honestly, it lines up with what I've been seeing on the ground. It's probably going to get a little bit worse before it gets better. They're now expecting Ontario home prices to finish the year down 3%.

Now here's why. Fixed-rate mortgages are on the rise, and the big banks and investors are betting that the Bank of Canada will raise its rates over the next year to get inflation under control. So borrowing is about to get more expensive, not less.

And on the ground, buyers are coming off the sidelines, but the deals happening right now lean in the buyer's favour. Sellers aren't getting their dream number. They're getting the price that they can stomach. However, CREA does expect things to pick up in 2027. So if you're buying, this could be your window. If you're selling, let's price it right from day one. What do you think's going to happen next with pricing?

videos.question: What is boating like in Midland and Tiny Township?
videos.short: Some of the best boating Ontario has to offer is right at your doorstep. Jonathan Wallace's first season at Wye Heritage Marina came with a pool, brand new pickleball courts, a dog park and a friendly marina community, and his favourite part was calm, sunny afternoons anchored off Beckwith Island.
videos.transcript:
Our boat came out of the water this week, and I'm absolutely so grateful. This was our first year at Wye Heritage, and it was absolutely amazing. The people here were friendly. We used the pool, we used the brand new pickleball courts, the dog park. We had fish and chips at Finn City. We even hosted the GBGH Gala in one of their hangars, and it was an absolutely beautiful venue.

But my favourite part was afternoons anchored at Beckwith Island. The sun was out, the water was calm. That was my summer.

Now, living in Midland and Tiny Township gives you some of the best boating Ontario has to offer. So if you've been thinking about getting on the water, it's right at your doorstep. Thank you to the marina team, our whole boating community, and all of our new friends on O dock. Spring can't come soon enough. See you on the water next year.

videos.question: Should I take my house off the market for the winter?
videos.card: Should I pull my house off the market for winter?
videos.short: Think twice before you do. Every fall a lot of sellers pull their homes, but buyers keep driving up from the city, so with fewer homes to choose from, yours gets noticed. Stay on through the first cold snap, maybe the second, because that is when people really change what they are doing. If things slow down and you truly believe taking it off is right, take it off, but don't step away while buyers are still looking.
videos.transcript:
Are you thinking about taking your home off the market today? Well, you should think twice before you do it. It's a beautiful day today. It's going to be 21 degrees. So before you call your realtor and say, let's try it again in the spring, hear me out.

And I get it. The last three winters up here have been really hard, and nobody wants to show a house in a snowstorm. So calling your realtor and saying, let's try again in the spring, sounds pretty good. But here's what happens every fall. Right around now, lots of sellers pull their homes from the market. Meanwhile, buyers keep driving up from the city. Everybody's out enjoying the warm weather, and the long-range forecasts are calling for a mild winter. So with fewer homes to choose from, yours gets noticed.

That's why I'd suggest you hang in there just a little bit longer. Stay on through the first cold snap, maybe the second. That's when people really change what they're doing. And if things slow down and you truly believe taking the home off the market is right, then take it off. But don't step away while buyers are still looking. If you're thinking about pulling your home for winter, think twice. Send me a DM if you want more information.

videos.question: What does the Bank of Canada rate hike mean for buyers and sellers on Georgian Bay?
videos.card: What does the rate hike mean for you?
videos.short: The quarter point increase, from 2.25% to 2.5%, is less about the size of the move and more about the message: the Bank of Canada is serious about inflation. Buyers holding pre-approvals may rush to use them first, then some will cool off as budgets shrink. For prices in Midland, Penetanguishene, Tiny, Tay and Wasaga Beach, nobody knows yet, but if buying gets harder to afford, prices could soften a little more.
videos.transcript:
Well, that's not the news anybody wanted. The rates, they just went up. The Bank of Canada just raised its key rate today for the first time since July of 2023. Now, it's only a quarter point, from two and a quarter to two and a half. So this isn't really about the size of the move, it's about the message. The bank is telling everybody that they're serious about fighting inflation. Gas, diesel and heating oil have all been really expensive for months, and they don't want that spilling into the price of everything else.

So what does that mean for buyers? In the short term, you might actually see a quick rush. People have already locked in pre-approval rates, and they'll want to use them before they run out. And then after that, some buyers may cool off a bit. Higher rates mean a smaller budget.

And for prices, honestly, nobody knows yet. If buying gets harder to afford, we could see home prices here in Midland, Penetang, Tiny, Tay and Wasaga Beach soften a little bit more. If you've been thinking about buying or selling and you're wondering what it means for you, send me a message.

videos.question: Did the rate hike make buying a home in Simcoe County more expensive?
videos.card: Did the rate hike make buying more expensive?
videos.short: Not necessarily. Your payment depends on the price and the rate, and Simcoe County prices are down about 3% in a year. On a $550,000 home with 5% down, the lower price saves about $90 a month while the higher rate adds back about $75, so the payment is still a little lower than last fall. You can always get a better rate later. You can never go back and change the price you paid.
videos.transcript:
The Bank of Canada just raised its rates by a quarter point, but buying a home here in Simcoe County actually just got marginally cheaper, and here's how it works. Your monthly payment depends on two things: the price of the home and the rate of your loan. When prices drop, you borrow less, and borrowing less can make up for that higher rate.

Now picture Sam and Jess. They're out looking at their first home this week for $550,000, and they find a house that they absolutely love. Then the news hits: rates are going up. Their first thought is, we just missed our chance. So we sit down and we run the numbers.

Prices in Simcoe County have dropped about 3% in a year, so that same house last fall would have cost them about $16,000 more. With a 5% down payment, that lower price saves them about $90 a month. Now, that higher rate does add back about $75 a month. So even after the increase, their payment is a little bit lower than it would have been last fall. And over a 25-year period, that lower price saves them about $26,000.

Now, nobody knows the bottom until prices start rising again, and buying isn't for everybody. But if you're in a good spot to own, the math is on your side right now. You can always get a better rate down the road, and you can never go back and change the price you paid.

videos.question: Should I wait until spring to sell my house in Midland?
videos.card: Should I wait until spring to sell?
videos.short: Waiting for spring feels safer, but it can cost more than you think when prices are trending down. The question worth asking is simple: if prices are lower in the spring, does that change your plans? Nobody has a crystal ball, but answering that honestly tells you what really matters.
videos.transcript:
Waiting until spring feels safe, but it could cost you more than you think. Now, let me tell you about Tom and Linda. Thirty years in their Midland home. Their kids' heights are still etched on the kitchen doorframe. Now the stairs are getting harder, and they're ready for something smaller and closer to their grandchildren.

They tell me, well, wait until the spring, my garden shows better. And I understand. It's a big step, and spring does feel safer. But right now, prices are trending in the wrong direction. So I asked them one honest question: what if the prices are lower in the spring? Will that change your plans for the future, or is that something you're going to be okay with? And they both went quiet, because nobody has a crystal ball. But that one question helped them decide what really mattered.

Now, no real estate agent wants to sell a home for less. Most of us got into this business because we care about people, and a lot of how we feel about our work comes from how we do for our clients. So I'd rather ask the hard question today than have them find out in six months. So if you have been thinking about waiting, let's sit down and talk through what it could mean for you.

videos.question: Why isn't my house selling?
videos.short: When the market slows, three things decide whether a home sells: the price, how it looks, and how many buyers see it. One home sat for almost a year, then sold in under 10 days with a new plan: fresh photos, staging, virtual furniture in the empty rooms, a video tour, drone photography showing the beach, and a price that stood out as one of the best deals around.
videos.transcript:
It sat on the market for almost a year, and then it sold in under 10 days. Same house, different plan. Now, the couple who owned it asked me one thing at their kitchen table: it's a beautiful home, why won't anybody buy it? It was putting their next move on hold, and the wait was costing them tens of thousands of dollars.

When the market slows down, three things decide if a home sells: the price, how it looks, and how many buyers ultimately see the property. Now, their photos were just average, so we started fresh with new photos. We brought in our stager to set up the rooms that already had furniture, and for a few empty rooms we added furniture to those photos digitally, so buyers could see how they could look. Then we put it everywhere buyers look, with a video tour and drone photography showing how close it was to the beach, and we priced it so that it stood out as one of the best deals around.

Under 10 days later it was sold, and they finally got to move on. So if your home's been sitting and no one's told you why, I'm happy to take an honest look.

videos.question: Should I list my house "as is, where is"?
videos.card: Should I list my house "as is, where is"?
videos.short: Usually not. Those four words sound safe, but buyers start picturing leaks or foundation problems and offer less, some walk away thinking you're hiding something, and the buyer's bank can start asking questions too. If something doesn't work, like the dishwasher, name just that one thing so buyers don't invent problems that don't exist.
videos.transcript:
Four words in your listing that can make buyers think the absolute worst: as is, where is. It means you're selling the home exactly as it sits, with no fixes. It sounds safe, but here's what it really does.

Buyers see those words and they start picturing leaks or foundation problems, and they offer you less money. Some get so nervous that they walk away completely, thinking that you're hiding something. And in my experience, the buyer's bank can notice it too, and they start asking what's wrong. So all that from a few words meant to keep things easy.

Here's the better way. If something doesn't work, like the dishwasher, name just that one thing, so that you don't have buyers inventing problems that don't exist.

videos.question: How do I buy my next home before I sell my current one?
videos.card: How do I buy before I sell?
videos.short: Make your offer conditional on selling your house by a set date, and add a pause clause. Without it, the seller can keep marketing their home and give you 24 to 48 hours to commit the moment another offer comes in, before your own sale is firm. The pause clause means that once you accept an offer on your home, the seller has to wait and can't bump you out, so your buyer commits, then you commit.
videos.transcript:
Need to sell your house before you can buy the next one? There's a way to do it without ending up homeless. Usually you make an offer on the new house, and it only goes ahead if you sell your house by a certain date. If it doesn't sell in time, the deal ends and you get your deposit back. Now, the catch is the seller gets to keep their house on the market. If another offer comes in, you get 24, maybe 48 hours to commit, or you lose it.

So picture a couple who finds the house that they've been waiting for. The seller says yes, and they list their home. A few weeks later they get an offer on their place, but that buyer still needs an inspection and bank approval. That same week, someone else comes and offers on the house they want. Now they only have 24 to 48 hours to commit to a house they can't afford yet. They could sell their home and have nowhere to go.

That's why we add the pause clause. Once you accept an offer for your home, the seller has to wait the duration of the pause clause, and they can't bump you out. Your buyer commits, then you commit, and you move into the house you wanted. So if you need to sell before you buy, send me a DM and I'll make sure you're protected.

videos.question: What should I do with a lowball offer on my home?
videos.card: What do I do with a lowball offer?
videos.short: Don't take it personally. Counter it and keep talking. What counts as a lowball depends on the home: $100,000 under on a $400,000 house is a huge gap, but on a million dollar home that has sat for six months it's a starting point. In Jonathan Wallace's experience buyers come up a lot once the talking starts. The first offer is where the deal starts, not where it ends.
videos.transcript:
That lowball offer on your home might be your buyer. When you list your home, you've got a number in your head, and that's normal. But the longer the home sits, the bolder buyers get. So say it's been six months, and an offer comes in a hundred thousand dollars under your price. It stings, and at first your thought is, absolutely not.

But what that means depends on the home. If your home is worth $400,000, well, that's a huge gap. But if your home is worth a million bucks, after six months, by my estimation, it really isn't a lowball offer. It's a starting point. That buyer is often thinking, we won't know if we don't ask. And in my experience, buyers come up a lot once the talking starts.

So if you're open to offers, you can't be offended by the first one. Don't take it personally. Counter it and keep talking, so the buyer feels that you're working towards the same goal. That's how both sides walk away with a successful deal. The first offer is where the deal starts, not where it ends.
